questions.stem: A 53-year-old client with COPD and schizophrenia tells the outpatient clinic nurse that during his last inpatient psychiatric stay, a technician restrained him in bed after he refused to give the technician his commissary money. What is the nurse’s priority action after assessing the client’s current safety?
options: Encourage the client to file a complaint himself if he still feels upset
Document the statement only, since the event happened during a past admission
Contact the technician directly to hear his side of the story before acting
Report the incident to the supervisor and protective agencies
optionRationales: Incorrect. Leaving reporting to the client shifts the nurse’s duty to a vulnerable client and may let abuse continue.
Incorrect. A past event still requires reporting; other clients may be at risk.
Incorrect. Investigating by contacting the alleged abuser is not the nurse’s role and may endanger clients or the investigation.

Correct. Restraint used to coerce a client is abuse and a severe boundary violation; the nurse reports to the supervisor/administration and protective agencies such as the state protection and advocacy agency.
questions.rationale: The client’s rights to control his possessions, to be free from restraint except in an emergency, and to be free from abuse and coercion were violated. The nurse documents his statements objectively and reports immediately through the chain of command and to appropriate protective and regulatory agencies. This is both microsocial advocacy (his safety) and macrosocial advocacy (exposing systemic abuse). A past event is still reportable because other clients may be at risk.
questions.takeaway: Coercive restraint is abuse — report it through the chain of command and to protective agencies, even if it happened in the past.
questions.hintContent: Does the passage of time remove the duty to report abuse?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client reports abuse by staff, choose reporting over investigating, waiting, or delegating the report to the client.

questions.stem: A nurse is writing an incident report about a colleague who appeared impaired during the shift. Which entries are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: “0710: Charge nurse notified; RN relieved of client assignment.”
“0705: Observed RN with unsteady gait and slurred speech at the medication cart.”
Charting in a client’s record: “Incident report filed regarding impaired RN.”
“The RN is obviously an alcoholic and has been for months.”
“0700: Odor of alcohol noted on the RN’s breath during handoff.”
optionRationales: Correct. Recording notifications and actions taken is appropriate.
Correct. Time-stamped, observable behavior is objective documentation.
Incorrect. Incident reports are not referenced in the client’s medical record.
Incorrect. This is a label and speculation rather than an observation.
Correct. An observed odor with time and context is a factual finding.
questions.rationale: Reporting must be objective: time, place, what was seen and heard, who was notified, and what actions followed. Labels such as “alcoholic” are conclusions the reporter cannot make and may be defamatory. Incident reports are quality and risk tools; the client’s record should contain client-care facts, not mention of the incident report.
questions.takeaway: Report what you saw, when, and whom you told — never labels — and keep incident reports out of the chart.
questions.hintContent: Which entries could another person verify by observation?
questions.hintStrategy: For documentation SATA, keep factual, time-stamped observations and eliminate opinions and misplaced entries.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old neighbor with a history of depression tells a nurse she is estranged from her only brother, who is her legal next of kin, and asks the nurse to be her health care decision-maker if she ever becomes incapacitated. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Of course. As a nurse, I can make sure your care is handled correctly.”
“State law doesn’t allow nurses to serve as anyone’s health care agent.”
“Your brother will make decisions no matter what documents you sign.”
“An attorney can help you name someone you trust as your health care agent.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Accepting blurs personal and professional roles and creates the conflict of interest the nurse should avoid.
Incorrect. This overstates the law; the concern is an ethical role conflict, and the statement would mislead her.
Incorrect. A valid health care power of attorney names an agent who takes priority over default next of kin.
Correct. Encouraging her to execute a durable power of attorney for health care and a living will naming a trusted non-nurse advocate protects her wishes and avoids role blurring.
questions.rationale: The nurse should act as a supportive neighbor, not the client’s clinician, and avoid blurring personal and professional boundaries. The course position is that serving as her proxy creates an ethical conflict of interest for the nurse. The most helpful response directs her to an attorney to complete a durable power of attorney for health care and a living will naming a trusted friend or other non-nurse advocate, which also ensures her brother does not decide by default.
questions.takeaway: When a friend asks a nurse to be their proxy, recommend a formal health care power of attorney naming a trusted non-nurse.
questions.hintContent: What legal tool lets a person choose someone other than next of kin?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate answers that are absolute or legally inaccurate; choose the one that empowers the person to act.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9

questions.stem: A nurse in North Carolina is caring for a 3-year-old with partial-thickness burns on both hands in a glove-like pattern. The parent states the child “pulled a pot off the stove,” a story that does not match the injury. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Wait for the skeletal survey results to confirm abuse before reporting
Ask the parent to explain the injury again to check for inconsistencies
Report the suspected abuse to the county department of social services
Tell the charge nurse and let her decide whether a report is needed
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof; waiting delays protection.
Incorrect. Questioning the parent to investigate is not the nurse’s role and may endanger the child.
Correct. Any person who suspects child abuse must report to the designated child protective agency (county DSS in North Carolina) without waiting for proof.
Incorrect. Notifying the supervisor per policy is fine, but it does not replace the nurse’s own legal duty to report.
questions.rationale: An immersion-pattern burn with an inconsistent history is a red flag for abuse. Nurses must report suspected child maltreatment to the designated child protective agency; in North Carolina, any person who suspects abuse, neglect, or dependency must report to the county DSS director. Reporters do not investigate or wait for proof, and good-faith reporters are immune. Telling the charge nurse is a tempting distractor, but internal notification does not satisfy the reporter’s personal legal duty.
questions.takeaway: Suspected child abuse: report it yourself to the child protective agency — suspicion is enough.
questions.hintContent: Does the reporting duty require proof, and can it be handed off?
questions.hintStrategy: Mandatory-reporting items reward direct reporting on suspicion; eliminate options that wait, investigate, or delegate the decision.

questions.stem: A nurse repeatedly skips barcode scanning when giving medications, stating, “It’s faster, and I always double-check the label anyway.” No client has been harmed. Using a Just Culture framework, how is this behavior best classified?
options: Human error, managed by consoling the nurse and fixing the system
At-risk behavior, managed by coaching the nurse on the risk
Reckless behavior, managed through disciplinary action
A conduct issue, managed by reporting diversion to the board
optionRationales: Incorrect. Human error is an inadvertent slip; this nurse chooses to skip scanning repeatedly.
Correct. Drifting from a safety practice while believing the risk is justified is at-risk behavior, managed by coaching.
Incorrect. Reckless behavior is conscious disregard of a known substantial risk; this nurse underestimates the risk rather than disregarding it.
Incorrect. There is no evidence of diversion, impairment, fraud, or another conduct issue.
questions.rationale: Just Culture distinguishes human error (inadvertent; console and redesign), at-risk behavior (a choice that drifts from safe practice because the risk is not recognized or seems justified; coach), and reckless behavior (conscious disregard of substantial, unjustifiable risk; discipline). Workarounds like skipping barcode scanning to save time are classic at-risk behavior. Reckless behavior is the closest distractor; the difference is whether the nurse recognizes the risk and consciously disregards it.
questions.takeaway: Workarounds rationalized as safe are at-risk behavior — coach them; reserve discipline for reckless disregard.
questions.hintContent: Is this an accident, a rationalized shortcut, or a conscious disregard of known danger?
questions.hintStrategy: For classification items, define each category in one phrase and match the behavior’s intent.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9

questions.stem: A nurse manager is reviewing practice events. Which situations involve conduct that should be reported to the state board of nursing in addition to being addressed by the employer? Select all that apply.
options: A nurse who charted a note late after assisting with a code
A nurse posting photos of a client’s wound on a personal social media account
A nurse in a romantic relationship with a current client
A nurse taking hydromorphone from wasted doses for personal use
A nurse who gave a scheduled medication 40 minutes late because of a rapid response call
optionRationales: Incorrect. Late charting due to an emergency, when properly labeled, is not misconduct.
Correct. Posting client images breaches confidentiality, a conduct issue reported to the board.
Correct. Sexual or romantic involvement with a client is a boundary violation reported to the board.
Correct. Drug diversion is a conduct issue reported to the board.
Incorrect. A delay caused by a competing emergency is a system issue handled within the facility.
questions.rationale: Drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches are conduct issues reported to the board of nursing rather than handled only by the employer. Practice events such as a delayed dose during an emergency or properly labeled late documentation are handled through the employer’s quality processes, often using a Just Culture approach. The distinction protects the public while avoiding punishment of system-caused events.
questions.takeaway: Diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary misconduct, and confidentiality breaches go to the board; system-caused practice events stay in quality improvement.
questions.hintContent: Which situations involve a choice that violates professional conduct rather than a delay caused by an emergency?
questions.hintStrategy: Separate conduct (intentional violations) from practice events (errors or delays from system pressures).

questions.stem: A nurse walking past a client’s room sees a nurse aide tying a confused older client to a chair with a bed sheet. The aide says, “Just until I finish my break, so she doesn’t wander.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Report the aide to the charge nurse before taking further action
Ask the aide to stay with the client until her break is over
Remove the sheet, stay with the client, and assess her for injury
Document the restraint and the aide’s statement in an incident report
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting is required, but the client is being restrained right now; stopping the harm comes first.
Incorrect. This does not remove the unlawful restraint and leaves the aide in charge.
Correct. The nurse first stops the ongoing harm by removing the improvised restraint and assessing the client, then reports to the supervisor.
Incorrect. Documentation is necessary but does nothing to stop the ongoing restraint.
questions.rationale: An improvised restraint used for staff convenience violates the client’s right to freedom from restraint except in an emergency and is a safety hazard (strangulation, falls, injury). When harm is happening in front of the nurse, the first action is to stop it and assess the client. The nurse then reports to the direct supervisor and documents objectively. Reporting first is the most tempting distractor because the chain of command is emphasized, but client protection takes priority when the harm is ongoing.
questions.takeaway: When harm is happening now, stop it first — then report up the chain.
questions.hintContent: Is the danger past, or is it still happening?
questions.hintStrategy: Safety-first items: choose the action that ends the immediate risk before reporting or documenting.
